problem.title: Design an Automated SLO-Driven Canary & Blue-Green Rollout Pipeline
problem.prompt: Design a zero-downtime deployment platform for 40 microservices handling 50k RPS, ensuring bad releases auto-rollback within 60 seconds without breaking active DB schemas.

spark.summary: An SLO-driven canary pipeline shifts traffic incrementally (5% -> 25% -> 100%) via Argo Rollouts/Envoy, auto-aborts within 60 seconds on 5xx or P99 regressions, and pairs with expand-and-contract DB schemas.
spark.keyTakeaway: Automate canary promotion against baseline-normalized SLOs (error rate and P99 latency), drain pods gracefully on rollback, and decouple destructive DB schema changes from code rollouts.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Across `40` microservices handling `50,000 RPS`, pushing a bad release to 100% of pods simultaneously causes a sitewide outage before an engineer can even open a dashboard.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts 5% Canary -> SLO Metric Gate -> Promote 100% or Abort <60s (CANARY_5% -> CANARY_25% -> PROMOTED_100% -> ABORT_0%); 60-Second Canary Evaluation & Instant Traffic Shift (Argo Rollouts -> Envoy / ALB -> Prometheus -> Baseline Pods).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Default Kubernetes `RollingUpdate` replaces pods based solely on `/readyz` health checks: **Blind to Business Latency**: A pod returning `HTTP 500` on `/checkout` or `800 ms` P99. Enterprise progressive delivery combines three layers: **Traffic-Weighted Canary (Argo Rollouts + Envoy/ALB)**: Shift `5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%` using L7 header/weight routing.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Automated canary and blue-green pipelines are standard across high-velocity engineering orgs: **High-Throughput APIs & Gateways**: Continuous deployment 50+ times/day without midnight release freezes.

learningJourney.title: Why automated canary rollbacks matter at 50k RPS
learningJourney.explanation: Across `40` microservices handling `50,000 RPS`, pushing a bad release to 100% of pods simultaneously causes a sitewide outage before an engineer can even open a dashboard. Automated progressive delivery exposes only `5%` of traffic to the canary, compares live 5xx and P99 metrics against the baseline every `15–30 s`, and rolls back in `< 60 s` without human intervention.

learningJourney.title: What happens with all-at-once rollouts and coupled schema changes
learningJourney.explanation:
Deploying without automated SLO gates and backward-compatible schemas creates three production hazards:

1. **100% Blast Radius**: A memory leak or bad config hits all `50k RPS` immediately.
2. **Slow Manual MTTR**: Waiting for pager alerts and manual `kubectl rollout undo` turns a 30-second glitch into a 15-minute outage.
3. **Broken Rollbacks**: If the new release ran `DROP COLUMN`, rolling back the binary crashes older pods.

sectionDiagram.summary: Argo Rollouts shifts Envoy/ALB weights back to 0% within seconds on any SLO breach while keeping baseline pods warm.

learningJourney.title: Naive solution (and why standard Kubernetes RollingUpdate falls short)
learningJourney.explanation:
Default Kubernetes `RollingUpdate` replaces pods based solely on `/readyz` health checks:

- **Blind to Business Latency**: A pod returning `HTTP 500` on `/checkout` or `800 ms` P99 latency still passes `/readyz` and rolls out to 100%.
- **No Baseline Normalization**: Static thresholds false-alarm during organic traffic spikes unless compared against the live stable baseline.
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Naive solution under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Enterprise solution: Argo Rollouts + Baseline SLO Gate + Expand-Contract DB
learningJourney.explanation:
Enterprise progressive delivery combines three layers:

- **Traffic-Weighted Canary (Argo Rollouts + Envoy/ALB)**: Shift `5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%` using L7 header/weight routing.
- **Automated SLO Judge**: Compare canary vs. baseline error rate (`canary_err > 2 * base_err` or `> 1%`) and P99 (`canary_p99 > 1.3 * base_p99`) every `15 s`; abort immediately in `< 60 s`.
- **Zero-Drop Pod Drain & Expand-Contract**: Use `preStop` sleep + graceful shutdown for zero dropped requests, and enforce backward-compatible DB migrations so rollback never breaks old code.

sectionDiagram.title: 60-Second Canary Evaluation & Instant Traffic Shift
sectionDiagram.summary: Shifting Envoy weights to 0% is instantaneous because baseline pods remain scaled and warm throughout the canary window.

learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.

learningJourney.title: Where SLO-Driven Canary Pipelines are used
learningJourney.explanation:
Automated canary and blue-green pipelines are standard across high-velocity engineering orgs:

- **High-Throughput APIs & Gateways**: Continuous deployment 50+ times/day without midnight release freezes.
- **Payment & Checkout Services**: Protecting conversion rates by auto-aborting latency regressions in `< 60 s`.
- **ML Model Serving**: Shadowing and canarying new model weights against live P99 and business KPIs.
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why should an automated canary judge compare canary error rate and P99 latency against the live baseline pods rather than using only fixed thresholds?

options.text: Baseline comparison normalizes for organic traffic surges or downstream hiccups that affect both versions equally, preventing false rollbacks
options.feedback: Correct: comparing canary vs. baseline isolates regressions actually caused by the new release.

options.text: Because Prometheus cannot store static threshold alerts
options.feedback: Prometheus supports static thresholds, but relative comparison avoids false positives during traffic shifts.

options.text: To allow destructive DROP COLUMN migrations during the canary step
options.feedback: Destructive schema changes still break rollbacks and require expand-and-contract.

_nextProblem.title: Designing Safe Liveness & Readiness Probes
_nextProblem.prompt: A Java Spring Boot order-processing service (24 pods on Kubernetes, HikariCP DB pool = 20, Tomcat max threads = 200) experiences a brief 4-second downstream Postgres lock contention. Because `/actuator/health` is wired to both `livenessProbe` and `readinessProbe` (`timeoutSeconds: 1`, `periodSeconds: 5`, `failureThreshold: 3`) and shares Tomcat's worker pool, all 24 pods fail liveness checks after 15 seconds. Kubelet kills and restarts all 24 pods simultaneously, causing a 6-minute outage due to 45-second JVM cold starts and cold-cache DB stampedes. Redesign the health-check and overload isolation architecture.

_problemQuestions.prompt: A user edits their bio and refreshes the page, only to see the old bio for 2 seconds because the read hit a lagging replica. Which consistency guarantee was violated?

options.explanation: Read-Your-Writes ensures a client always observes its own completed writes.
The write was durable on the primary; the replica simply lagged.
Atomicity governs all-or-nothing commit, not cross-replica visibility.

_problemQuestions.prompt: Why does placing `request_timestamp` at the very beginning of a 3,000-token system prompt hurt latency and cost?

options.explanation: BPE still tokenizes the text normally.

options.text: It invalidates prefix/KV caching for all subsequent 3,000 tokens on every request
options.explanation: Correct! Prefix KV caching requires an exact token match from index 0 onward.
Output length is unaffected; Prefill cache reuse is what breaks.
